comment_text: Here in the US, as mentioned, the fair market value (FMV) of the products you receive for reviews under the Amazon Vine program is treated as "taxable income". Some people initially think that they will only have to pay "sales tax" on the product value, however in reality you (and the IRS) will receive a 1099-NEC for income tax filing, so how much you end up paying the government depends on your income tax bracket, not your States sales tax rate. This of course normally then also increases your state and local income taxes as well. Also per the Vine program rules you must keep the product and not destroy, give away or sell it for at least 6 months. Only then you can dispose of it as you wish. Not a bad program but you need to remember the tax consequences. You get the products "free" all year and people tend to go overboard, but then find out afterwards that they've created a tax problem for themselves.

comment_text:
I was aware of the shady reputation of the store, but decided to order something inexpensive to check it out. I ordered a kit for a ham antenna auto-tuner that came to less than $20 shipped. I actually got it in 10 days, which isn't bad. However, they use very misleading product pages with photos of items that mislead you into believing that these items are included. I had believed the case was included because it was shown along with all the kit parts, but it wasn't. It did not state anywhere that the case wasn't included. They also use thumbnails that show items with a great price, but when you click them, it isn't that item but some small accessory on the same page. The actual product you saw is 100x that price. eBay seems to do this as well and they claim this is just how product pages function when there are multiple options to choose from. I call B.S. to this and that it is intentional click bait.

Anyway, I needed then to order the case for the project and did so. It came from a different seller. After ordering, I went back to ask the seller a question about the item and the page wasn't there, nor was the seller. I messaged the place I bought the kit from and they checked and said that seller was "fake" and had "stolen" their photos and was not authorized to sell that little metal case. They told me this was very common in China. I had been tracking the delivery from their website and after about nine days, it said "Delivered", although it had not been. I tried to dispute the transaction on AliExpress, but here's the catch: You have to wait over 30 days before you can even file a dispute and then, as this video states, it takes two more weeks to get a refund. I'm not waiting 45 days just to get a refund so I filed a dispute with PayPal.

"Fool me once, shame on you. Fool me twice, shame on me."

I will not be using AliExpress again and I suggest you do not. The "deals" are not really that good, many of the items are fake, and the risk is just too great.

comment_text:
The time to file a dispute has changed. For example, I currently had to file a dispute over non-delivery. The estimated delivery window was 60 days from shipment. After 40 days, and then again on the 59th day, I tried filing a dispute. The system would not let me. It stated I must wait until after the last day of estimated delivery date and then I would have 15 days to file a claim. So I waited until day 61, whereas it finally allowed me to file a dispute. 

It looks like this also coincides with how they verify shipments being received as well. All my orders show that if I do not verify I have received my shipment within the estimated delivery date, AliExpress will automatically mark it as received 15 days after the estimated delivery date. So what that means is they have generally set a time period of 15 days after the estimated delivery date to either verify you have received the product, and/or file any claims/disputes over it. It is a much clearer system then they had before.

Also- the biggest sign of fraud that occurs on Aliexpress that I have experienced is the seller requesting you to close the claim/dispute. They will ask you to wait longer for the product, or will work out a refund through PayPal, or will promise to send a replacement. DO NOT EVER CLOSE YOUR DISPUTE. The seller knows that if you close your dispute, you will no longer have any rights to reopen it if there are problems. The seller also knows by asking you to "wait a little longer", you could pass your dispute time. And NEVER agree to refund money through Paypal. They can easily refund you through AliExpress. Them asking you to close your claim/dispute, is almost always them manipulating you so they do not have to make things right.

comment_text:
This is certainly a fun video, as you are very charismatic on camera, a few things just rubbed me the wrong way. 
1: You seem to be reviewing things that are out of your area of expertise for too little time. For the two subscription boxes, you only reviewed one box which will not give you a good judge of their quality and worth. Additionally, you ordered the Crunch Labs box meant for younger kids? 
2: You glossed over the fact that the $600 lightsaber replica (the cheapest lightsaber replica they sell is still close to $200 and probably also dropshipped) is simply a $300 replica with mp3s loaded onto it and double the price. That is a scam.
3: The JLaser product is (to the best of my research) also a dropshipped product
4: For the Clicks keyboard, you didn't buy the most recent model, you bought what is essentially a 2 year old prototype and made it seem like it's all the company offers. You also didn't bother to get in contact with TheMrMobile (or any of the other youtubers featured in the video, I can safely assume since you wouldnt contact everyone else except him) to ask about his product where, as he says in his own comment, he would have been more than happy to show you around his product
5: Why were you reviewing candy on a tech-oriented video? It seems like there may have been some bias there since you said you were pretty good friends with Ryan. Pizzafy is also a confusing inclusion for a tech-focused video
6: When reviewing Jerry's knife, you tested the sharpness of the blade, which isnt even the selling point of the knife. The high quality construction and stability when holding the industry standard blades is what sets it apart. 
7: Panels did not deserve even half of the score you gave it considering the exact same functionality can be gained by going to Google images (for free, too!)

tldr; This video felt rushed and not to the same standard of quality of other videos. Lack of complete transparency with products combined with poor research makes it feel like a filler episode only meant to get views, not to inform the viewer.

comment_text: Great points overall, but I'd actually caveat how I approach the acknowledging emotions point. I've found that it's too easy to misunderstand or misidentify the customer's emotion, which could make the whole interaction worse. If you say "I can understand how frustrating that could be," and they respond with "I'm not frustrated at all... ", their immediate thought is "you're not getting me". Instead, you should just side with them against the issue "That sounds like a nightmare, I'm so sorry you've had to deal with that, I'm here to help you get sorted." Their next thought is "this person gets me". So the approach is to include yourself in their world, and not analyze it from the outside. Just my two cents.

Sorry, but you don't sell a product just because it solves a problem. This mantra, too often repeated by infopreneurs, is too extreme. Fortunately, the world doesn't just move on the basis of what we need, but also on the basis of what we want. People buy things because they like them, because they're passionate about them, because they've fallen in love with them, because they resonate with something deep inside them. 
I know it because it's all around us. You don't buy a Netflix subscription because it solves a problem. You don't buy expensive or cheap paintings to decorate your home because it solves a problem. You don't go to the cinema or to Disneyland because it solves a problem, you don't buy a cake or a candy because it solves a problem. You don't buy comics or manga or a novel because it solves a problem. You don't read science or History books because it solves a problem. You don't travel on holidays because it solves a problem. 
Now, you can say that all these stuff can be seen as a solution to problems, but it just distorting the sense of words to make them fit into your own categorization, kind of playing on words. 
Those are desires, which are always somehow rooted in deep needs which take their origins in problems, but those are not the kind of problems you're talking about. 
There are plenty of shops on Etsy or Amazon selling digital or physical products and making tons of money out of it, but their products are not a solution to any kind of problem.

As someone who worked at Amazon, I can tell you these are just bulk-produced items that got sent to any big company willing to handle them.  The ones missing stuff or without proper packaging were most likely customer returned items that were sent back to the originally seller to do with whatever they deemed. A lot of sellers will simply resell them "as is" whereas Amazon itself goes through a damage/return process. 

A lot of the time sellers will dump their products at warehouses and refuse to handle any returns or damages or even refuse to take them back (I've seen products sit for 9+ months), but usually Amazon will gather returned or damaged items and ship them back to the seller if there are issues. It's a headache with drop-shipped and mass produced items tbh. An incredible waste of everyone's time, money, and energy imo.

There's ONE BIG flaw in the system here in the UK. If, on eBay,  you want to sell a £3,000 Heuer for example, there is no courier in the UK who will insure it FROM you or the Post Office TO the authentication centre.  Secursus (a specialist watch insurer) even refuse too.  DPD, Fedex, UPS, DHL etc won't insure it and some say in their T&C's they won't ship watches. Royal Mail Special Delivery only insure up to £2500 and if a £3000 value watch goes missing then technically they do not have to pay out as it's over their limit. 
I believe that the only way eBay themselves can ship watches FROM the authentication centre to RECIPIENTS is that they have a corporate underwritten insurance policy.   
I'm not knocking eBay authentication as a recipient but the initial part of the chain (at least here in the UK -((I think the US has better insurance limits)) is flawed and would prevent many many non business sellers selling a watch from their collection through eBay.

The most common scam lately, that I've run into twice this year is a 
fake tracking and delivery scam,
done by sellers.
They send a package far too light and too small (to be your item), to someone else's house in your town, so they can have cheap tracking to give to eBay.

The speaker, Jessica Apotheker, is a marketer who is interested in the impact of generative AI on marketing.

She argues that generative AI will have a major impact on marketing, but that it is important for marketers to be prepared for this change.
One of the ways that generative AI will impact marketing is by automating many of the tasks that are currently done by humans. This will free up marketers to focus on more strategic work.
Another way that generative AI will impact marketing is by personalizing content to a much greater extent than is currently possible. This could lead to more effective marketing campaigns, but it could also lead to content overload for consumers.
Apotheker argues that the key to success in the age of AI is for marketers to develop a "left AI brain" in addition to their right AI brain. The left AI brain is responsible for data analysis and logic, while the right AI brain is responsible for creativity and intuition.
Apotheker also argues that it is important for marketers to protect their brand identity in the age of AI. This means being careful not to let AI generate content that is inconsistent with the brand's values.
Finally, Apotheker advises marketers to focus on what they are good at. If you are a creative person, then focus on developing your creative skills. If you are a data-driven person, then focus on developing your data analysis skills.

I went though this what they now call 'no buy challenge' years ago, during my high school years, because I noticed I was spending and spending but the joy disappeated quickly every time.
After recognizing this pattern, I said to myself I won't be buying anything for three years.
When I achieved this goal, I was 19.
And so, right after that, because I didn't know what clothes suited me - and what clothes to buy - I went straight to gain knowledge about it from an image consultant, who explained to me what suited my body type and the colors and all of that.
I took that as my basis and I started carefully purchasing again taking into account my lifestyle.
Gradually I understood what garments would complement me the best and now I have a healthy relationship with shopping.
I concede myself something every now and then, which we call statement pieces, but since I know myself inside out I can take a leap of faith and having a shopping adventure without it turning dysfuncional.

comment_text:
I used to buy a lot of unnecessary low cost make up when I was a student. It was a rough time for me and even just going out to buy cheap stuff made me feel better for few hours. It was also around 2014/2016 and makeup used to be more structured, you felt you need more products. But one day I realized I had lot of bad quality stuff I never used, and all together the cost was important for a student with low income like I was. So I decided to throw everything away and I set myself some rules: 1 item per type of product, no doubles, no palettes but only single eyeshadows I choose (so I realized that I actually need no more then 8 shades), never buy new stuff unless the old one is finished or expired, buy only things that you like to use, even in makeup don't follow trends you don't like or are not made for your skin type (I never liked to countour, glass skin looks bad on me). 
This way I can invest in fewer better products and I am having fun again with makeup. I keep buying regularly because I do finish what I have and I change what I don't every 2 years or so because they expire, but I don't feel guilty anymore because I feel very conscious of what I do. I think now I spend around 100€/year which I think It's pretty fair for a fullface with good products.

video_title: How to Treat Compulsive Shopping
comment_text:
Compulsive shopping - very dangerous. Often a symptom and indication of DEEP rooted psychological issues including depression that could lead to suicidal thoughts and eventual suicide even! Many shopping addicts use the 'liberating' exciting feelings that accompany the anticipation of shopping - to cover their underlying trauma. I know someone who is a full blown shopping addict. They find excuses to go to the grocery store every single day and bring home stuff worth $200 or $300 dollars.

 Additionally packages keep being delivered at the door. 'Oh, I thought another grinder would be good for the kitchen' is the explanation. So mixer/grinder number 3 gets setup in the kitchen right next to the other two that work just as well. A few days later a set of pestle and grinding stone also get delivered to the house and they sit right next to the 3 grinders. 

'Oh, this stone and pestle will help make delicious guacamole.' Always a reason, always an excuse. Slowly the kitchen and pantry and porch get overrun with utensils and storage bins with even more items, overflowing from the Kitchen where we have run out of space. 

Any outing with them results in this grown up person coming up with another reason/idea to stop at a grocery store or restaurant, 'Oh, I just remembered that there is this ONE item that we need at home. Promise, I will run in and bring just that one item and be back in 5 minutes'. Well the 5 minutes expands to an hour or more before this person steps out with bags and bags of items, most all of which are not needed'. 

It was only after I accompanied this person to Walmart and other large grocery stores, that I realized why Walmart and other retail outlets place some select items strategically at the entrance to the grocery section. This person will instinctively gravitate towards those loaves of freshly baked long bread and say: 'Hey lets grab some of these' [when there are several of these that lay unused at home, some of them moldy, because this person brings more and more of these every visit they make to the store'. So if I were to say, 'Hey we have so many of them at home', this person will just smile and brush it off and say, 'No problem, just grab a few more'.

This individual has piles of very costly clothing that they purchased from high end retail outlets and never used them ONCE. So what do they do with all these high value but unused coats, jackets etc.? After a few years, they pick them up and give them away to someone [with the price tag and packaging still intact. So the item was not even taken out of the packaging!]. And why do they give these clothes away? To make room in the overflowing closet for even more new clothes! Most of the new clothes will never be used.

Left untreated this mental disease progresses. Over a couple of decades or so, the behavior patterns of this person can become more erratic. Sudden burst of temper tantrums [where this person used to be very even tempered and balanced, originally]. Other bizarre behavior patterns. Thoughts and talks about taking their own life. That life holds no meaning. And then more frenzied bouts of shopping. The thought, preparation and anticipation of the shopping trip is the greatest even of their day and life. Sadly, as the shopping ends and they have to lug their purchase to their car, their excitement level comes crashing down. The 'Hypo mania' turns instantly into a 'depressive' mood-swing as they pull up to their house. The thought of lugging their new purchase into the house is very 'depressing to them'. The excitement level was in the anticipation, the preparation, the selection of items at the store, and the transaction, the swiping of the credit card, the collecting of the items and putting them back into the shopping cart. But there the excitement begins to taper off. And in some case 'guilt' overtakes their mind - as most of them are aware of their shopping addiction, even though most will try to deny an delude others and themselves from accepting that they have issues inside that manifest outside in the form of their 'shopping addiction'.

Which is why many of the shopping addicts, rush back into the store after dropping their original purchase in their car. They hate the 'crashing' depressive feeling and the onslaught of guilt that comes with the end of the shopping trip. So they try to switch back from the 'depressive' state to the 'hypo manic'/super-excited state, by going back to purchase that 'one' item that they forgot. Well, the one item become 5 or 25 more items. Then they wistfully drive back home.

Many of the purchased items may never be used. This could be confusing to people around them. 'Why would anyone buy items excitedly and never use them or rarely use them. Or not show the same excitement in using them as they did in the planning of the purchase?' - people may wonder. But the answer lies in the fact that the 'anticipation' the 'process', the 'transaction', the 'sight and smells' at the stores, the drive to the shopping store, these are what trigger the excitement. Not the actual item or the consumption of it. True many times they are excited about opening the packaging and using the item. Or unpacking the grocery item and cooking it. But by and large, it is the shopping experience that is paramount. The overriding thrill. So items soon lose value in their mind, once they are home. After all you can always go and buy more of them, to repeat the shopping experience and the excitement that comes with it.

comment_text:
The "wait to buy" hack, so far, has been the most helpful for me. I wont pick things up and walk aroubd with them, either. When I want to grab an item, I tell myself to wait and then if I'm still thinking of it the next day (or at the end of the shopping trip) I can reevaluate and consider biying it. Every single time, more than half of what I desperately wanted I've forgotten about by the next day, even sometimes within 5 minutes! 
I also have a hack where I ask myself "if this were $5, would you buy it?" More often than not, I wouldn't.  Since $5 is a small and easy amount to spend, it helps me realize what I actually value vs. what just entices me in the moment.
